title: Machine Learning Under Constraint (Part 3): De-Risking Near the Profit Target and the News-Window Rule
text:
Table of Contents
Introduction
Derisking Near the Profit Target
Interaction with the Remaining-Risk Budget
Funded-Stage News Constraint
Making the Calendar Symbol-Aware
Implementation Notes
Conclusion
Attached Files
Introduction
Part 1
generalized the prop-firm rules a sizer enforces into an explicit
PropFirmRuleSet
, and gave
PropFirmAccountState
a
current_balance
that accumulates correctly across an entire challenge — every trading day's realized P&L and fees, banked forward through every
reset_daily()
call.
Part 2
built the modifier that reads the downside half of that state:
WParamCalibrator
takes
risk_budget_pct
, the fraction of the loss budget still remaining, and flattens the sizing sigmoid as it is consumed.
This article completes
PropFirmAwareSizer.size()
's modifier chain with two further modifiers.
derisking_factor
reads
phase_progress
(how much of the profit target has already been reached) and reduces position size as that target approaches, protecting accumulated progress rather than remaining capital.
risk_budget_pct
and
phase_progress
are distinct quantities, though not statistically independent: both are computed from the same balance and P&L path, and they can move together or apart. An account can be flush with loss budget while also close to finishing its challenge.
news_window_factor
reads neither state. It reads the clock and a calendar of event times, under a rule specific to the funded stage of a challenge rather than the evaluation stage. It is a sizing heuristic layered on that rule, not an implementation of the rule's profit accounting, and the calendar's own accuracy matters more than the function's small size would suggest.
Derisking Near the Profit Target
Why Protect the Ceiling
A phase profit target under
FundedNext's Stellar 2-Step rules
is 8% for the first challenge phase — accumulated gradually, typically across weeks, not won in a single session. Reaching it converts a fixed evaluation fee into a funded account with an open-ended profit share, the convex payoff
Part 1
opened with. That framing motivates a sizing rule once progress nears the target: an unconstrained Kelly fraction has no mechanism to recognize that the account is holding something valuable and close to cashing in, and sizes the next trade identically whether the account is at 10% of its target or 95%. Protecting a near-complete pass is a different problem from protecting remaining capital, which is why it needs a second modifier reading a second signal, one derived from the same account history but measuring something different, rather than a more elaborate version of the first.
The option analogy is a motivation, not an argument. An account near its phase target resembles a deep in-the-money option, and one intuition is that the marginal upside from another trade is small next to the downside of a reversal that pushes the account back through the target. The analogy does not determine the sizing curve. The right behavior for an option depends on time to expiry, volatility, the holder's utility, and the exercise rules, and none of those implies a linear reduction between 80% and 100% of the target.
derisking_factor
is a piecewise-linear heuristic chosen for simplicity; it prices none of the option's mechanics.
derisking_factor
The function is a piecewise-linear heuristic: flat at full size until 80% of the phase target, then declining to a floor at 100%. The floor depends on whether the account has already satisfied the rule set's minimum trading-days requirement. The curve's effect on pass rate and expected value is untested in this article.

Table 1. derisking_factor at representative phase-progress points, both floors
As established in
Part 1's Opinion
, the 80% threshold and both floors are a strategy choice about how aggressively to protect an in-hand pass, independent of which firm's rules are in force.
meets_min_trading_days
is different: it is a fact about the account's progress against a firm rule, not a tunable strategy choice, discussed below. The function otherwise takes no rule set, no account reference, and no phase — the same design pattern
Part 1
used for
news_window_factor
, a pure function that is trivially unit-testable with primitive inputs.
Choosing a threshold and the two floors.
80%, 0.30, and 0.10 are starting values, not tested or universal ones. As a working hypothesis, a high-win-rate, low-variance strategy has little reason to protect progress early, since most of its trades near the target are themselves low-variance, so a later threshold and shallower floors cost little. A strategy that relies on occasional large wins — a lower win rate, fatter tails — has more to lose from one badly timed reversal wiping out weeks of progress, and benefits from de-risking earlier and further. The threshold and floors are not a minor stylistic knob; they are a strategy parameter like any other.
Why
meets_min_trading_days
Is an Input, Not a Tunable Default
derisking_factor
takes
meets_min_trading_days
as a required argument rather than folding it in as a third tunable default next to the 80% threshold and the two floors. The distinction is not cosmetic. The threshold and floors are a strategy choice, as above.
meets_min_trading_days
is a fact about the account's current standing against
PropFirmRuleSet.min_trading_days
, sourced from the property
Part 1
added to
PropFirmAccountState
, and the two-floor policy chosen here cannot be evaluated without it. A single-floor policy would not need the flag; the argument is required by this design, not by the rule set.
The two floors reflect one design decision. While the minimum trading-days requirement is still open, the strategy keeps a higher floor (0.30) so that it can keep accumulating trading days. Once the requirement is met, the floor drops to 0.10. The 0.30 value is not derived from any firm rule. Firms define a qualifying trading day in different ways, and if a day qualifies with any executed trade, no particular size is required. In that case 0.30 carries more risk than the rule demands. Check how your firm defines a trading day, and set
floor_days_unmet
to the smallest size that qualifies.
0.10 is a starting point, not a derived optimum, and it has no rule-based justification. Once the target is reached and the trading-days requirement is met, the pass condition is satisfied, and further exposure adds risk without advancing it (subject to how the firm evaluates and closes the phase). A floor of 0.0, which stops trading at that point, is the policy most consistent with that objective. The 0.10 default keeps a small exposure alive and is a placeholder; pass
floor_days_met=0.0
to go flat.
Whether 80%/0.30/0.10 improves pass rate or expected value versus constant sizing is an empirical question this article does not answer; it trades a certain cost (forgone size late in a challenge) against an uncertain benefit (protection against a reversal that would have failed the challenge anyway), and resolving it needs backtesting across many simulated attempts rather than reasoning about the curve's shape alone.
Interaction with the Remaining-Risk Budget
What Happens When Both Modifiers Are Active
WParamCalibrator
responds to
risk_budget_pct
: how much room remains before failure.
derisking_factor
responds to
phase_progress
: how close the account is to success. A good day, late in a challenge, is exactly the scenario where these pull in different directions rather than agreeing:
The derisking_factor curve and its interaction with the budget-driven ceiling
Figure 1. Two-panel illustration of the derisking curve and its interaction with the budget-driven ceiling
Left panel
:
derisking_factor
against
phase_progress
for both floors — flat below 80%, then separating to 0.30 or 0.10 depending on
meets_min_trading_days
.
Right panel
: a simulated account starting at 87.5% phase progress, having a good day with no material losses.
cal_bet_size
— the budget-only ceiling from Part 2 — stays near its 0.98 cap throughout, since the daily limit keeps expanding with the day's profit. The combined ceiling,
cal_bet_size × derisking_factor
, falls from about 0.72 to 0.47 as
phase_progress
climbs to 94.8%.
The right panel answers the question Part 2's conclusion deferred:
WParamCalibrator
alone would size this account up, because the budget genuinely supports it.
derisking_factor
pulls the other way, and both act on the final size, because
PropFirmAwareSizer.size()
multiplies every modifier together rather than taking a minimum:
combined_modifier = sigmoid_scale × derisking × news
(
news
, covered in
Section 4
, follows the identical rule but depends on neither budget nor phase progress). Multiplication is not
min()
. Every active modifier below 1.0 keeps reducing the result, so two moderate restrictions combine into a tighter one than either alone: modifiers of 0.8 and 0.7 give 0.56, not 0.7. No modifier needs to know the others exist, which keeps each one independently testable, at the cost of compounding restrictions rather than applying only the strictest.
Multiplication has a second consequence: the same combined ceiling can arise from two different account situations, and
final_size
alone does not say which. A budget at 1.4% remaining with 90% phase progress, and a budget at 0.91% remaining with 20% phase progress, both combine to exactly 0.637: one account close to finishing and safe on capital, the other early and running low on capital, arriving at the identical position size. The diagnostic columns returned by
PropFirmAwareSizer.size()
—
cal_bet_size
,
derisking
,
w_param
— are required to tell the two cases apart.
This demonstrates one deliberately favorable day. When both signals tighten at once, for example after a large intraday loss that leaves the account close to its target, the reductions compound. Test the combined ceiling against your own configuration before trusting it near both boundaries at once.
Production Note: One State Snapshot Per Event
PropFirmAwareSizer.size()
computes
derisking
once per call, from a single
PropFirmAccountState
snapshot, and applies it uniformly across every event in whatever batch is passed to that call. This is correct for a live strategy calling
.size()
once per bar with a freshly updated state. It is incorrect the moment
.size()
is called once across a batch of events spanning more than one meaningfully different
phase_progress
— precisely what a vectorized backtest tends to do.
# Wrong: one snapshot, never advanced, sizes the whole window from the initial state
state = PropFirmAccountState(initial_balance=
100_000.0
, phase=phase, rule_set=rules)
sizing = sizer.size(events=all_events, prob=all_probs, pred=all_preds, state=state)
# Correct: before each event, apply only P&L from trades that closed before its entry
state = PropFirmAccountState(initial_balance=
100_000.0
, phase=phase, rule_set=rules)
closed = realized_pnl.sort_index()
# indexed by trade close time
costs = fees.reindex(closed.index, fill_value=
0.0
)
cursor, rows =
0
, []
for
ts
in
all_events.index:
    n = closed.index.searchsorted(ts, side=
"left"
)
if
n > cursor:
        state.update(realized_pnl_delta=closed.iloc[cursor:n].
sum
(),
                     unrealized_pnl=
0.0
,
                     fees_and_swaps=costs.iloc[cursor:n].
sum
())
        cursor = n
    rows.append(sizer.size(events=all_events.loc[[ts]], prob=all_probs.loc[[ts]],
                           pred=all_preds.loc[[ts]], state=state, current_time=ts))
sizing = pd.concat(rows)
The corrected version replaces one vectorized call with a Python-level loop over events. Its cost is usually small next to model training and label computation, but it is not negligible in general. For a large event-level backtest the loop can become the bottleneck, so profile it before assuming otherwise. It is also the only version where
state.phase_progress
at each call reflects the account as it stood at that point in history.
Two details of the loop matter. It applies only P&L from trades that closed strictly before the event's entry time, because updating the state with an event's own outcome before sizing it is look-ahead bias: the size would be computed after the result is known. It also indexes P&L by trade close time, so overlapping positions do not leak their eventual outcomes into events that opened while they were still running. The sketch passes
unrealized_pnl=0.0
and omits the daily reset for brevity. A production loop marks open positions to market and calls
state.reset_daily()
at each day boundary, which is also what advances the trading-days count behind
meets_min_trading_days
.
The dangerous direction is a stale snapshot, typically the initial one, applied uniformly: every late-window event, where
phase_progress
was genuinely near 100% and should have been suppressed toward the floor, gets sized as if
derisking_factor
were still 1.0. That means the account takes its largest, least-restricted positions exactly when closest to a completed pass, which is what
derisking_factor
exists to prevent. It also produces no error, warning, or obviously wrong number. Only a comparison against the correct per-event calculation reveals it.
The opposite mistake, applying an end-of-window snapshot uniformly, fails differently.
phase_progress
is near its maximum for the whole window, so every early event is suppressed using information that was not available when it was sized. That is look-ahead bias, and it understates early-window sizes.
Funded-Stage News Constraint
What FundedNext Actually Restricts
FundedNext restricts nothing during the Challenge Phases, on any Stellar model. Once an account transitions to the FundedNext Account, a News Reward Share Rule applies: trades opened or closed within five minutes before or after a listed high-impact news event have only 40% of their profit counted toward the account balance, for a symmetric ten-minute window. Losses inside that window count in full; only profit is haircut. In accounting terms, a trade opened or closed inside the window credits 0.4 × P&L when P&L is positive and the full P&L when it is negative. Existing positions can be held through a news event without restriction, since the rule triggers on execution, not on merely being in a trade while news prints. The rule also applies only to news that
directly correlates with the traded pair
— FundedNext's own example: a EUR/USD trade during high-impact USD or EUR news is subject to the haircut; the same trade during high-impact CNY news is not.
news_window_factor
The function is a short, phase-gated window check that converts every timestamp to UTC first (see Timestamp Normalization):
def
news_window_factor(
    current_time: datetime,
    news_times:
list
[datetime],
    news_profit_credit:
float
,
    window_minutes:
float
=
5.0
,
    phase: Phase = Phase.CHALLENGE_PHASE_1,
) ->
float
:
if
phase != Phase.FUNDED
or
not
news_times
or
news_profit_credit >=
1.0
:
return
1.0
window = pd.Timedelta(minutes=window_minutes)
    ct = _to_naive_utc(current_time)
for
nt
in
news_times:
if
abs
(ct - _to_naive_utc(nt)) <= window:
return
news_profit_credit
return
1.0
The phase gate follows the rule's scope: challenge-phase calls exit immediately at
1.0
, since FundedNext documents no news restriction there.
window_minutes
defaults to
5.0
and is used as a half-width, reproducing the documented ten-minute total window without a separate before/after pair.
news_profit_credit
comes from
PropFirmRuleSet
, per
Part 1's
argument for keeping firm-level facts on the rule set rather than hardcoded here.
The rule is an accounting rule, and
news_window_factor
does not implement it. The function returns a size multiplier for an entry evaluated at
current_time
, which is a trading policy layered on the rule. The two differ in three ways:
Payoff shape
: scaling a position by 0.40 scales profit and loss alike. A full-size trade inside the window would credit 0.40 of its profit and all of its loss. The scaled trade credits 0.16 of the full-size profit and 0.40 of the full-size loss. The multiplier trades reward for lower loss exposure, so it is a conservative heuristic, not an exact model.
Closing events
: the rule also triggers on closes, and the function sees only
current_time
. A position opened outside a window that closes or is stopped out inside a later one is not covered.
Execution type
: the function cannot tell an entry from an exit, or from an existing position being held through the news. Call it for entry sizing only. Exits inside a window need separate handling by the calling code.
The news-window step function and the symbol-correlation gap
Figure 2. Two-panel illustration of news_window_factor's behavior
(a)
:
news_window_factor
across a 40-minute window. The challenge-phase line stays flat at 1.0; the funded-phase line drops to 0.40 for exactly the documented ten minutes and returns to 1.0 immediately outside it.
(b)
: a EUR/USD trade at the exact moment of a JPY-only event. An unfiltered calendar haircuts it to 0.40 by mistake; a symbol-filtered calendar (
Section 5
) correctly leaves it at 1.00.
How Often Does This Actually Matter?
A step function confirms the mechanism works; it says nothing about how often a real trading day intersects a news window. The answer hinges on one question: does the strategy's entry timing have anything to do with when news gets released?
An illustrative year of USD high-impact events (NFP, CPI, and the eight FOMC decisions, 32 events total) gives something to test two trading patterns against. Both trade sets are synthetic.
How often trade timing collides with a news window
Figure 3. Two-panel illustration of the news-window collision rate by strategy type
(a)
: 780 trades/year with entry timing unrelated to the news calendar land in a news window
zero
times over the simulated year. 616 trades/year from a news-reactive breakout strategy land in a news window 3.25% of the time.
(b)
: splitting the reactive strategy's trades by origin shows where that comes from. The 96 trades placed deliberately after a release collide 19.8% of the time; the other 520, unrelated to any specific event, collide at 0.19% — indistinguishable from panel (a).
In this illustration, the collision rate depends on the strategy's timing, not on the rule. A strategy whose entries are unrelated to the calendar, such as a carry strategy or a session-open breakout, collided with a news window zero times in the simulated year. That is one draw from a rare-event process. It shows the rule can go unmet for a year; it does not show the effect is immaterial, and only collisions were simulated, not the cost of the haircut. Repeat the simulation across many seeds, and use your own trade timestamps and news calendar, before concluding that modeling the rule can be skipped. A strategy built around trading the volatility that follows a release met this rule on purpose, in roughly one of every five deliberate entries. For that strategy, the news rule directly taxes the trades the strategy exists to take.
Making the Calendar Symbol-Aware
Why Naive Calendars Are Wrong
news_times
is typed as
list[datetime]
, a flat list of moments, with no instrument, currency, or event identity attached.
news_window_factor
checks only whether
current_time
falls within the window of any entry; it has no way to ask whether an entry has anything to do with the symbol being sized, because that information was never in the calendar to begin with. Feeding it an unfiltered global calendar — the natural shape of most third-party economic calendar feeds — produces the wrong answer whenever a currency-irrelevant event falls inside a position's window, inflating the collision rate (
Section 4
) with false positives on every symbol traded.
Filtering by TransactionCostModel Currencies
The fix does not belong inside
news_window_factor
itself; teaching it about currency correlation would bolt a second responsibility onto a function whose entire value is being trivially easy to reason about. The fix belongs upstream, and it turns out to almost already exist.
Part 14's
TransactionCostCollector.mq5
reads
SYMBOL_CURRENCY_BASE
and
SYMBOL_CURRENCY_PROFIT
from the broker's own symbol specification and writes both to its export CSV.
TransactionCostModel
never read them —
load_cost_model()
stopped at
symbol
,
digits
,
point
,
pip_factor
,
tick_size
,
tick_value
, and
contract_size
. The currency fields were collected, written to disk, and silently discarded on the Python side.

Run against Figure 2(b)'s scenario — a EUR/USD cost model,
correlated_currencies
=
{"EUR", "USD"}
, a calendar with both the EUR event and the JPY-only one —
filter_news_by_cost_model
keeps the EUR event and drops the JPY one, reproducing the 1.00 FundedNext's rule says should apply. This is broker-verified rather than hand-typed, covers every FX symbol a cost model has already been collected for, and avoids a second source of truth for a fact
TransactionCostModel
already holds. The fix required no change on the MQL5 side: the collector has exported these fields since its first version; the gap was three missing reads on the Python side.
Scope.
Base and profit currency are a sound relevance key for FX pairs and a weaker one elsewhere. An index CFD, a metal, an energy contract, or a crypto CFD responds to news that its quote currency does not capture: for XAUUSD, XAU is not a calendar currency, and USD is only a partial proxy. Events tied to a common currency or to global releases may also not map to a single ISO code. Whether the firm treats such news as correlated with a symbol is the firm's determination. For non-FX symbols, replace
correlated_currencies
with an explicit per-symbol mapping rather than relying on the specification fields.
A Companion Collector for the Calendar
filter_news_by_cost_model
needs a calendar, and the official
MetaTrader5
Python package has no binding for MQL5's Economic Calendar functions at all — a gap confirmed on MQL5's own forum. MQL5's documentation also states that calendar functions cannot be called inside the Strategy Tester, returning
FUNCTION_NOT_ALLOWED
on every attempt. The fix follows the same pattern this series already uses for transaction costs: export from an MQL5 script, load the CSV in Python.

, attached below, follows the same shape as
TransactionCostCollector.mq5
and the same five-column CSV format, resolving each calendar value to its event and country for the ISO currency code the filter above uses, keeping only events at or above a configurable importance threshold:

already expects:

the IANA name of the server's clock and has no default; returned timestamps
are timezone-aware UTC. Ambiguous or nonexistent DST-transition times raise.

Timestamp Normalization
current_time
and every entry in
news_times
must be UTC, but nothing in the original
news_window_factor
checked that. The call
pd.Timestamp(current_time).tz_localize(None)
strips whatever timezone label a timestamp carries without converting to a common reference. That is correct if every input is UTC. It is silently wrong for any timezone-aware timestamp in another zone.
# What tz_localize(None) does: strip the label, keep the wall-clock number
# What it does NOT do: convert to UTC first
pd.Timestamp(
"2026-01-01 07:00"
, tz=
"-05:00"
).tz_localize(
None
)
# -> 07:00, not 12:00
The function listed in Section 4 now calls a small helper instead. It converts timezone-aware inputs to UTC and treats naive inputs as UTC:
def
_to_naive_utc(ts) -> pd.Timestamp:
    ts = pd.Timestamp(ts)
if
ts.tzinfo
is
not
None
:
        ts = ts.tz_convert(
"UTC"
)
return
ts.tz_localize(
None
)
This is worth singling out rather than applying universally, because a timezone mismatch produces a plausible-looking wrong number with no exception anywhere. The input type is unusually easy to get wrong when crossing a Python, pandas, and MQL5 boundary, and unusually hard to notice once wrong. The helper still trusts naive timestamps to be UTC, so a naive server-time timestamp would pass unnoticed.
The calendar collector is where this stops being abstract: its timestamps are trade-server time by MQL5's convention, not UTC. Making
server_tz
a required keyword-only argument of
load_calendar_csv
means the conversion cannot be skipped by omission, and the loader returns timezone-aware UTC. It does not verify that the zone is correct. A fixed-offset zone such as
Etc/GMT-2
is right only for a server that does not observe daylight saving; many broker servers shift with it, so use the IANA zone that matches the server's clock changes, and confirm it with the broker.
Conclusion
Key takeaways:
Remaining risk budget and phase progress are distinct signals, not independent ones.
Both derive from the same balance and P&L history. A good day late in a challenge is where they pull in opposite directions, and treating them as one signal misses that.
Multiplying modifiers compounds them; it does not select the strictest.
Every modifier below 1.0 keeps reducing the size, so two moderate restrictions combine into a tighter one, and no modifier needs to know the others exist.
The same combined ceiling can come from opposite situations.
The diagnostic columns, not the final number, are what tell them apart.
meets_min_trading_days
is a fact about the account, and only the two-floor design needs it.
The threshold and floors around it are strategy parameters, and none of them has been tested against pass rate here.
The news rule applies only in the funded stage and only to news correlated with the traded pair.
The phase gate and the symbol filter implement those two limits. The size multiplier itself is a heuristic; it does not model the profit haircut or closing events.
Whether the news rule matters depends on the strategy's entry timing.
In the illustrative simulation, timing-independent entries collided zero times in a year and deliberate post-release entries about one time in five. One simulated year is not evidence that the rule can be ignored.
Symbol-aware calendar filtering is needed for FX pairs.
An unfiltered calendar adds false positives on every symbol, and the currency-based key does not extend cleanly to indices, metals, energy, or crypto CFDs.
Collectors and loaders are version contracts, not just file formats.
A collector script can change its section names and its swap-mode spellings without warning, and a loader that assumes the old shape fails silently rather than loudly.
Timestamps carry a timezone contract.
Calendar times are trade-server time. The loader now requires the server's timezone and returns UTC.
The three modifiers covered across this article and Part 2 — budget, phase-progress, news — complete
PropFirmAwareSizer.size()
's current design.
Part 4
moves to a different kind of constraint entirely: not on how large a position can be, but on how wide its stop-loss is allowed to sit, where the prop-firm daily loss ceiling meets the optimal trading rule search from
Part 15
.

for: derisking_factor is a piecewise-linear heuristic: flat at full size until 80% of the phase target, then declining to a floor at 100%

The function otherwise takes no rule set, no account reference, and no phase — the same design pattern Part 1 used for news_window_factor, a pure function that is trivially unit-testable with primitive inputs
The 80% threshold and both floors are a strategy choice about how aggressively to protect an in-hand pass, independent of which firm's rules are in force
The threshold and floors are not a minor stylistic knob; they are a strategy parameter like any other

Whether 80%/0.30/0.10 improves pass rate or expected value versus constant sizing is an empirical question this article does not answer; it trades a certain cost (forgone size late in a challenge) against an uncertain benefit (protection against a reversal that would have failed the challenge anyway), and resolving it needs backtesting across many simulated attempts rather than reasoning about the curve's shape alone
news_window_factor is a short, phase-gated window check that converts every timestamp to UTC first
A strategy built around trading the volatility that follows a release met this rule on purpose, in roughly one of every five deliberate entries

How often trade timing collides with a news window — Figure 3(a): 780 trades/year with entry timing unrelated to the news calendar land in a news window zero times over the simulated year; 616 trades/year from a news-reactive breakout strategy land in a news window 3.25% of the time

Figure 3(b): splitting the reactive strategy's trades by origin shows where that comes from — the 96 trades placed deliberately after a release collide 19.8% of the time; the other 520, unrelated to any specific event, collide at 0.19%

against: В торговом сигнале используется будущее: в разделе 'Production Note: One State Snapshot Per Event' прямо указано, что при векторизованной батч-обработке (например, в бэктесте) использование единого снапшота состояния для всего окна событий приводит к применению устаревшего значения phase_progress — например, значение 100% достигается только в конце окна, но все события в окне (включая те, где phase_progress был 95%, 98%, 99.9%) обрабатываются с начальным значением, т.е. derisking_factor = 1.0. Это означает, что позиции на последних барах, где по логике должен быть резкий спад размера, фактически открываются на полном размере — сигнал использует *будущее состояние* (уже достигнутый target) для определения момента де-ризинга, но при этом не обеспечивает корректного учёта этого состояния *по времени*, а полагается на внешнюю (и легко нарушаемую) семантику вызова. Автор признаёт это как 'look-ahead bias' в случае обратной ошибки и как 'dangerous direction' в случае прямой — но сама функция derisking_factor требует актуального phase_progress, который зависит от P&L, рассчитанного *после* входа, а не до него.

Правило нельзя записать точной формулой: в статье отсутствуют чёткие условия входа в сделку. Вся статья посвящена *модификаторам размера позиции* (sizing), а не правилу генерации сигналов. Нет ни одного упоминания о том, *когда* открывать позицию: нет описания индикаторов, условий пересечения, фильтров тренда, подтверждения, стоп-уровней или даже базовой стратегии (например, breakout, mean-reversion). Упоминаются лишь абстрактные 'synthetic trades', 'news-reactive breakout strategy', 'carry strategy', но без формализации. Функции derisking_factor и news_window_factor — это *пост-процессоры* размера, а не торговые правила. Введение говорит: 'completes PropFirmAwareSizer.size()\'s modifier chain', а не 'defines entry logic'.
non_fatal: Требуются данные, которых нет у спот-форекса: в разделе 'Making the Calendar Symbol-Aware' описана необходимость использования экономического календаря с привязкой к валютам (EUR, USD), включая время событий и их важность. Спот-форекс не предоставляет официальный экономический календарь; он является внешним источником (третьи стороны, MQL5-скрипты), но это не делает правило фатальным — календарь доступен и может быть загружен отдельно.

В основе мартингейл, сетка или усреднение убытков: в статье нет ни слова о мартингейле, сетке, усреднении, добавлении к убыточным позициям или изменении размера позиции на основе исхода предыдущих сделок. Размер регулируется только текущим состоянием счёта (risk_budget_pct, phase_progress) и внешними факторами (новости), но не по результату конкретной предыдущей сделки.

Статья не про торговое правило, а про инфраструктуру: хотя статья действительно фокусируется на sizing-логике и инфраструктуре (календарь, сбор данных, UTC-нормализация), она *прямо заявляет цель* — 'De-Risking Near the Profit Target and the News-Window Rule', то есть представляет собой часть торгового правила (условия изменения размера как составная часть стратегии). Однако ключевой порок — отсутствие самого правила входа — уже учтён в 'against' как фатальный пункт (2).

judge.reject_reason: Статья не описывает торговое правило входа: отсутствуют чёткие условия открытия длинной или короткой позиции (направление, индикаторы, уровни, фильтры, подтверждение). Вся статья посвящена модификаторам размера позиции (sizing) — derisking_factor и news_window_factor — которые применяются *после* генерации сигнала, но сам сигнал не определён. Это фатальный порок: правило невозможно записать, так как нет входного условия. Также в derisking_factor используется phase_progress — параметр, зависящий от накопленного P&L, который в реальном времени доступен только *после* закрытия сделок; при векторизованной обработке в бэктесте это приводит к look-ahead bias — функция требует актуального состояния счёта, но не гарантирует его корректного временного выравнивания без внешнего цикла, что делает детерминированное применение на закрытых барах невозможным без дополнительной, неописанной логики.
judge.summary: Статья описывает два модификатора размера позиции — derisking_factor (снижение объёма при приближении к целевому профиту) и news_window_factor (снижение объёма при торговле в окне новостей), но не содержит ни одного условия для генерации торгового сигнала входа. Функции являются пост-процессорами sizing, а не правилами входа, и их применение зависит от динамического состояния счёта (phase_progress), которое в бэктесте требует строгого пособытийного обновления — условие, не реализуемое детерминированно на закрытых барах без внешней логики.
